lesson.title: Same Cliff, Shorter Ladder: How Catalysts Reshape the Energy Diagram
lesson.summary: On a reaction coordinate diagram, a catalyst lowers the height of the activation energy peak, or replaces one tall peak with a series of smaller ones, while leaving the starting and ending energy levels, and therefore delta H, exactly where they were.
lesson.body:
Draw the catalyzed and uncatalyzed pathways for the same reaction on one diagram and they share the same starting point, the reactants' energy, and the same ending point, the products' energy. Since delta H is just the difference between those two fixed points, it is identical for both pathways: a catalyst never touches the thermodynamics of a reaction. What differs between the two curves is the height of what sits in between. The catalyzed pathway's highest point is lower than the uncatalyzed pathway's peak, meaning Ea for the forward reaction is smaller with the catalyst present. Because the transition state's energy is what actually changes, and both the forward and reverse activation energies are measured relative to that same peak, the catalyst lowers the reverse activation energy by the same amount as well. That is precisely why, as the next chapter makes explicit, a catalyst cannot shift where a reaction's equilibrium sits: it speeds up getting there, not the destination itself.

In practice, a catalyzed pathway is often not simply the same single hump made shorter. More commonly, the catalyst opens up an entirely different mechanism, one built from several smaller steps and intermediates, forming a catalytic cycle where each individual step has a lower barrier than the one big barrier of the original, uncatalyzed, single step pathway. On the diagram this shows up as multiple smaller peaks and valleys instead of one tall peak. The highest point among all of those smaller humps is the effective activation energy of the catalyzed route as a whole, the same rate determining step idea from earlier in this unit, just now applied to a catalytic mechanism, and it is that highest point which needs to be lower than the original uncatalyzed peak for the catalyst to actually speed things up.

It is worth seeing numerically just how much a modest drop in Ea matters, since the relationship between activation energy and rate is exponential rather than linear. The Arrhenius equation states that the rate constant k equals A times e raised to the power of negative Ea over RT, with R the gas constant and T the temperature in kelvin. Consider an illustrative case: suppose an uncatalyzed reaction has Ea equal to 75 kilojoules per mole, and a catalyst lowers that to 50 kilojoules per mole, a drop of 25 kilojoules per mole, at room temperature, 298 kelvin. The ratio of the catalyzed rate constant to the uncatalyzed one works out to e raised to the power of 25000 divided by the quantity 8.314 times 298, which is e raised to about 10.1, or roughly 24000. In other words, even though Ea only dropped by about a third, the reaction proceeds on the order of twenty four thousand times faster, because Ea sits inside an exponent, so a comparatively small change in barrier height produces an enormous change in rate.

This is the mechanism behind everything discussed in the catalysis chapter: it is precisely because activation energy controls rate so sensitively that even a catalyst which only trims the barrier by a modest amount can turn a reaction that is imperceptibly slow into one that runs to completion in seconds. The one point worth holding onto above all others is that a catalyst reshapes the middle of the diagram, the pathway, and never the two endpoints, the elevations of the reactants and the products.
